newsitem.title: UK: Singer & Friedlander aims to grow earnings for biz unit and screens.
newsitem.headline: Singer & Friedlander aims to grow earnings for biz unit and screens.

text.p: British investment bank and fund management group Singer & Friedlander Group Plc on Tuesday reported increased pretax profits and said it would continue to grow earnings per share (EPS).
"EPS growth continues. I'm very pleased with the rate at which it is growing," chief executive John Hodson told Reuters, adding that this was largely due to the strength of its core businesses.
The group announced a 22 percent increase in pretax profits for 1996, to 41.7 million pounds from 34.2 million, and a 17 percent rise in EPS to 11.63 pence from 9.96 pence a year earlier.
But the results received a cool response from the market. The group's shares were down 10.5 pence at 141 pence at 1315 GMT.

Hodson said Singer & Friedlander's main profits during the year had come from its stockbroking business. Favourable conditions in both the Nordic and British stock markets meant brokers Carnegie made 16.0 million pounds while British operation Collins Stewart made 7.6 million pounds.
Carnegie made profit before tax of 14.3 million pounds in 1995 while corporate finance, broking and fund management had "delivered the goods", he said.
Collins Stewart has a very low fixed cost base, made markets in around 100 companies and was a very specialist and very successful business, Hodson said.
It was involved in 22 deals during 1996 and raised more than 300 million pounds for corporate clients. Collins Stewart now acts for 45 companies.
Hodson said Singer had built up its fund management business and now had six billion pounds of funds under management. This showed a significant rise from the 3.8 billion pounds of assets in 1995.

"We've now got a group that is building to a decent critical mass," Hodson said. Interest in fund management meant that prices were too high to contemplate buying a funds business and Singer would instead build its share of discretionary funds.
In his results statement, Singer's chairman Anthony Solomons said the group was still looking for opportunities to expand its operations. He said these would have to meet its strict criteria.
But Hodson played down the likelihood of Singer making further acquisitions to grow. He said Carnegie and Collins Stewart would both grow organically.

During 1996 Singer took a 3.0 million pound capital loss on the sale of its insurance broking business Edgar Hamilton Group, which during the part of the year it was owned by Singer made a loss of 0.3 million pounds.
But the company made a healthy profit from the sale of its stake in the Peoples Phone Company Plc. This gave it a profit of 9.8 million pounds over cost and a book profit of 16.4 million pounds.
Singer said this reflected the success of its policy taking strategic stakes in "carefully selected companies".
The group said it would pay a final dividend of 2.8 pence and a total of 4.65 pence for the year, compared with 4.0 pence in 1995.
